newsitem.title: USA: Talks continue as GM Pontiac strike drags on.
newsitem.headline: Talks continue as GM Pontiac strike drags on.

text.p: Talks continued over the weekend to resolve a General Motors Corp. pickup truck plant strike, which stretched into its 68th day Sunday -- one day longer than a 1970 walkout over a new national contract.
"I'm not proud of that, but you got to do what you got to do," said Ron Miller, president of United Auto Worker Local 594 in Pontiac, Mich.

About 5,800 hourly workers at GM's Pontiac East truck assembly plant and nearby product development operations walked off the job at midnight April 22 when talks on a new local agreement broke down. A new three-year national pact was reached last November.

The two sides held intensive negotiations last week, and Miller said Sunday some progress has been made. There are now resolutions to more than 3,000 of the 3,660 grievances the union had lodged against GM, the world's largest automaker.
But negotiators are still at odds over the central issue in the strike: staffing levels.

The Pontiac East facility is the lead plant for the next generation full-size pickup truck. GM has said the new vehicle will require 30 percent fewer workers to produce. Production is slated to begin next June.
Miller said his members need more workers now to relieve overtime strains. For example, he said, some members have 26 and 27 years of seniority but cannot get time off to take a vaction.
"GM says they need to cut people. We're in a position here where we can't cut people," he said.
GM spokesman Dan Flores declined to characterize the discussions, which resumed on Sunday morning.
"Negotiations are continuing toward reaching a tentative agreement," he said.
The strike means GM is entering its annual two-week summer shutdown Monday with the costly walkout and about 15 other local agreements still unresolved.
The Pontiac plant is one of five GM facilities in North America that make full-size pickup trucks. Analysts estimate GM has lost production of more than 50,000 pickup truck units.
The company loses about $8,200 on each vehicle it does not make out of Pontiac East, according to CSM Forecasting Inc, a Farmington Hills, Mich., consulting firm.
As of mid-May, GM said the Pontiac strike and a earlier one in Oklahoma City, Okla., had cost it $225 million in profits.

By not being on the job at the start of the shut-down, Local 594 members could end up sacrificing one week of holiday pay and one week of vacation pay they would normally get. Strikers have been receiving $150 a week in strike pay.
If an agreement was reached Sunday, Miller said, it would be impossible for production to resume Monday because many workers are not around.
"I don't think half of the people are in town," he said.
Since the beginning of this year, the company has been hit by a total of five strikes -- three by UAW members and two by members of the International Union of Electronic Workers.
